overview.title: A new target: generalization power and the efficiency ratio
overview.main_topic: Figure 19.8 (skill vs. task-relevant information for systems of different generalization power), the proposal to target generalization power itself, intelligence defined as an efficiency ratio, and the introduction of ARC-AGI
overview.central_idea: Skill at a fixed task can be raised by adding information, so it can't measure intelligence. Instead, fix the information (priors plus experience) a system gets and measure how well it handles tasks sufficiently different from anything it saw, tasks its creators couldn't anticipate. Intelligence is the ratio between that information and the resulting range of handled novel situations.
overview.importance: This is the book's positive proposal after the critique of p.602-603: a precise definition of intelligence and an evaluation protocol for it, which ARC-AGI implements (p.605-608).
learning_objectives: Read Figure 19.8 and explain how it supports the claim in its caption
Explain why the goal 'create a model that solves task X' triggers the shortcut rule
State the definition of intelligence as an efficiency ratio and identify its two terms
Describe the two conditions for measuring this ratio fairly (fixed information, unanticipated test tasks)
prerequisites: The shortcut rule and 'buying' skill with data (p.602-603)
The difference between skill and intelligence (p.603)
Train/validation/test splits and why test data must be unseen

summary:
**Figure 19.8** plots *task-specific skill* (vertical axis) against *task-relevant information, priors + experience* (horizontal axis) for systems with different **generalization power** (= 1, 2, 3, and a steep curve labeled = N). Each system's skill rises as it gets more information. A green dashed line marks *fixed priors + experience*: at that fixed amount of information, systems with more generalization power reach more skill. The caption draws the other conclusion: a **low-generalization system can achieve arbitrary skill at a fixed task given unlimited task-specific information**. So skill alone can't tell you which curve a system is on.

**19.3.4** proposes the remedy. To make AI able to deal with the variability of the real world, stop seeking *task-specific skill* and target **generalization power itself**. The field needs new metrics of progress that point in the right direction and give actionable feedback. As long as the goal is "create a model that solves task X," the shortcut rule applies and you get a model that does X, period.

The author's definition: intelligence is an **efficiency ratio**, the conversion ratio between the *amount of relevant information* you have about the world (past experience or innate prior knowledge) and your *future operating area*, the set of novel situations in which you'll produce appropriate behavior (your *skill set*). A more intelligent agent handles a broader set of future situations with less experience.

To measure it: **fix the information** available to the system (experience and priors), then measure performance on reference tasks **sufficiently different** from what it has seen. Maximizing this ratio should lead toward intelligence. To avoid cheating, test only on tasks the system wasn't programmed or trained for, tasks its *creators could not have anticipated*.

In 2018-2019, the author developed the **Abstraction & Reasoning Corpus for Artificial General Intelligence (ARC-AGI)** (footnote: Chollet, "On the Measure of Intelligence," 2019) to capture this definition (continued on p.605).

paragraphs.excerpt: Figure 19.8 A low-generalization system can achieve arbitrary skill at a fixed task given
paragraphs.what_it_says: The caption: a low-generalization system can achieve arbitrary skill at a fixed task given unlimited task-specific information. The figure plots task-specific skill against task-relevant information (priors + experience) for curves labeled generalization power = 1, 2, 3 and N, with a green dashed line at 'fixed priors + experience'.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Each curve is one system. Moving right along a curve means giving the system more information about the task; moving up to a higher curve means a more intelligent system. A given skill level (a horizontal line) can be reached by any curve, just at a different horizontal position. The steep 'N' curve reaches high skill with very little information. Only at a fixed amount of information (the dashed vertical line) does skill rank the systems by generalization power; the dotted horizontal mark there shows the skill one curve reaches at that budget.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It is the visual version of p.603's argument: a benchmark that lets systems use unlimited data measures how much data they got, not how intelligent they are. It also shows how to fix that: compare skill at fixed information.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: this is like comparing learning curves (accuracy vs. training-set size) across algorithms. A fair comparison of sample efficiency fixes the training-set size.

terminology.meaning: Everything the system gets that bears on the task: built-in priors plus experience (training data).

paragraphs.excerpt: To make AI actually intelligent and give it the ability to deal with the
paragraphs.what_it_says: To make AI able to deal with the variability and changing nature of the real world, move away from task-specific skill and target generalization power itself. We need metrics of progress that point in the right direction and give an actionable feedback signal. As long as the goal is 'create a model that solves task X,' the shortcut rule applies and we get a model that does X, period.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Research is guided by its metrics: a metric is a feedback loop that tells researchers whether an idea helped. If the metric rewards skill on a fixed task, ideas that add data or task-specific engineering look like progress. A metric of generalization would only reward ideas that improve the ability to handle novelty.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the 'right target' the section title refers to and the rationale for ARC-AGI.

terminology.meaning: A metric that changes in response to real improvements, so researchers can tell which ideas work.

p.606: ARC-AGI later gave a clear signal of the shift to test-time adaptation

paragraphs.excerpt: In my view, intelligence can be precisely quantified as an efficiency ratio: the conversion
paragraphs.what_it_says: Intelligence is an efficiency ratio: the conversion ratio between the amount of relevant information about the world (past experience or innate prior knowledge) and the future operating area, the set of novel situations where you'll behave appropriately (your skill set). A more intelligent agent handles more future situations with less experience. To measure it, fix the information (experience and priors) and measure performance on reference tasks sufficiently different from what the system had. Maximizing the ratio leads toward intelligence. To avoid cheating, test only on tasks the system wasn't programmed or trained for, which its creators couldn't anticipate. In 2018-2019, the author developed ARC-AGI to capture this definition.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The ratio has an input (information: priors + experience) and an output (the range of novel situations handled). Fixing the input turns the ratio into a performance measure on novel tasks. The 'creators could not have anticipated' condition closes a loophole: if developers can foresee the test tasks, they can put information about them into the system (through training data or design), which moves the system along its curve rather than up to a higher one. It's the familiar rule of not training on the test set, applied to the developers' own knowledge, not only to data.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This gives a definition precise enough to build a benchmark around. The emphasis on priors is new: two systems are only comparable if they start with the same prior knowledge, which ARC-AGI handles with Core Knowledge priors (p.605).
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: in 'On the Measure of Intelligence' (2019), Chollet formalizes this with algorithmic information theory, weighting skill across a scope of tasks by generalization difficulty and normalizing by priors and experience. The book gives only the verbal version.

concepts.name: Generalization power
concepts.definition: How much skill a system can extract from a given amount of task-relevant information (priors plus experience), particularly on situations unlike those it has seen.
concepts.intuition: The height and steepness of a system's curve in Figure 19.8.
concepts.technical: Can only be read off skill when information is held fixed; otherwise more data can substitute for it.
concepts.significance: The book proposes it as the target of AI research, instead of task-specific skill.
concepts.example: A human learns a new board game from a few explanations and games; a low-generalization system needs millions of games.
concepts.misconception: That higher benchmark skill implies higher generalization power.

concepts.name: Intelligence as an efficiency ratio
concepts.definition: The conversion ratio between the relevant information available (experience and innate priors) and the future operating area (the set of novel situations handled appropriately).
concepts.intuition: How much new capability you get per unit of information.
concepts.technical: Measured by fixing priors and experience and evaluating on reference tasks sufficiently different from the information provided, which the creators couldn't anticipate.
concepts.significance: Makes intelligence measurable and gives a direction to optimize.
concepts.example: Two systems with equal scores on a new task: the one that got less experience and fewer priors is more intelligent.
concepts.misconception: That a ratio rewards small systems with little skill. The numerator is the breadth of novel situations handled, so no skill means no intelligence.

concepts.name: Priors (prior knowledge)
concepts.definition: Knowledge a system has before any task experience: innate knowledge in humans, built-in design in AI systems.
concepts.intuition: What you bring to the test before seeing the first question.
concepts.technical: Counts as task-relevant information on the horizontal axis of Figure 19.8, so it must be controlled for when measuring intelligence.
concepts.significance: Hardcoding task-specific priors is one way to buy skill without intelligence.
concepts.example: Translation equivariance built into a convnet is a prior about images.
concepts.misconception: That only training data counts as 'information given' to a system.

concepts.name: ARC-AGI
concepts.definition: The Abstraction & Reasoning Corpus for Artificial General Intelligence, a benchmark developed by Chollet in 2018-2019 to measure intelligence as defined on this page.
concepts.intuition: An IQ-test-like set of novel grid puzzles that can't be memorized ahead of time.
concepts.technical: Fixes priors (Core Knowledge) and tests on tasks unseen and unanticipated (p.605).
concepts.significance: The book's concrete implementation of the new target.
concepts.misconception: That it measures acquired knowledge; it deliberately avoids it.

math.title: Intelligence as an efficiency ratio (verbal definition written as a ratio)
math.source_text: intelligence can be precisely quantified as an efficiency ratio: the conversion ratio between the amount of relevant information you have available about the world (which could be either past experience or innate prior knowledge) and your future operating area

variables.meaning: The set of novel situations where the agent can produce appropriate behavior (its skill set).
Innate prior knowledge plus past experience.

math.operations: A ratio of output (breadth of handled novelty) to input (information). The book states 'conversion ratio between information and operating area'; written as output over input so that larger means more intelligent, matching 'a broader set of future tasks... using a smaller amount of past experience.'
math.purpose: Turns 'intelligence' into a quantity that can be compared and maximized.
math.interpretation: Raising skill by adding information leaves the ratio unchanged or lowers it; only better generalization raises it.
math.intuition: Miles per gallon for learning: how far you can go in new territory per unit of experience.
math.numerical_example: Purely illustrative: agent A solves 60 of 100 novel tasks after 10 demonstration examples; agent B solves 60 after 1,000. Same skill, but A's ratio is 100 times higher, so A is more intelligent by this definition.

deeper.title: Reading Figure 19.8
deeper.body:
- **Vertical axis**: task-specific skill.
- **Horizontal axis**: task-relevant information = priors + experience.
- **Curves**: one per system, labeled generalization power = 1, 2, 3, and a steep curve = N. Higher curves reach more skill for the same information.
- **Green dashed vertical line**: 'fixed priors + experience', a fixed information budget. Along this line, skill ranks systems by generalization power.
- **Caption**: with unlimited information, even a low curve can be pushed to high skill on a fixed task.

Hence two ways to compare systems: measure skill with free access to information (which rewards whoever adds the most data), or measure at a fixed budget (which rewards generalization). The book argues for the second.

deeper.title: The 'creators could not have anticipated' condition
deeper.body:
Beyond the book, why this condition matters:
1. Suppose a benchmark's tasks are public and stable.
2. Developers, consciously or not, put knowledge of these tasks into the system: data that resembles them, architectures suited to them, hand-written heuristics.
3. That's task-relevant information that wasn't counted, so the system moved right along its curve in Figure 19.8.
4. Its score goes up without its generalization power going up.

This is test-set leakage at the level of the research process. Private, held-out test sets (as ARC Prize uses) are the defense.

deeper.title: Fuel efficiency
deeper.body: Judging a car only by how far it drove tells you little if one car got a full tank and another a cup of fuel. To compare engines you fix the fuel and measure the distance. Figure 19.8's dashed line is the fixed fuel; skill on unseen tasks is the distance.

visualizations.title: Illustrative version of Figure 19.8: skill vs. information
visualizations.why: Reproduces the shape of Figure 19.8 so you can compare the curves at a fixed information budget (x = 2) and see how low-power systems need much more information to reach the same skill. The curve formulas are invented for illustration; the book's figure is qualitative.

title.text: Skill at a fixed information budget ranks systems by generalization power

misconceptions.claim: A system with higher skill on a benchmark has more generalization power.
misconceptions.correction: Figure 19.8 shows that a low-generalization system can reach any skill with enough task-specific information. Skill only ranks systems when information is fixed.

misconceptions.claim: Testing on a held-out split of the same dataset measures intelligence.
misconceptions.correction: The book asks for tasks 'sufficiently different' from what the system had access to, which its creators couldn't anticipate. A held-out split of the same task measures skill on that task.

misconceptions.claim: Prior knowledge doesn't count as information given to the system.
misconceptions.correction: The definition explicitly counts 'past experience or innate prior knowledge' as the information side of the ratio.

earlier.note: Refers to Figure 19.8: engineers can buy skill with data or hardcoded knowledge.
Efficiency as the core of intelligence; the shortcut rule.

takeaways: Figure 19.8: given unlimited task-specific information, even a low-generalization system reaches arbitrary skill, so skill can't measure intelligence.
The new target is generalization power itself, not task-specific skill.
Intelligence is an efficiency ratio between information (priors + experience) and the range of novel situations handled.
Measure it by fixing priors and experience and testing on sufficiently different tasks the creators couldn't anticipate.
ARC-AGI (2018-2019) was built to implement this definition.

questions.question: In Figure 19.8, under what condition does task-specific skill reliably indicate generalization power?
options: When task-relevant information (priors + experience) is fixed
When the task is fixed and well known in advance
When the system has the most parameters
questions.answer: When task-relevant information (priors + experience) is fixed
questions.explanation: At the dashed 'fixed priors + experience' line, higher curves give higher skill. With unlimited information (option 1), any curve reaches high skill. A fixed, known task (option 3) is exactly what allows skill to be bought. Parameter count isn't on the figure.

questions.question: What are the two quantities in the book's efficiency ratio?
questions.answer: The amount of relevant information available (past experience or innate prior knowledge) and the future operating area (the set of novel situations where the agent will produce appropriate behavior).
questions.explanation: Stated in the second paragraph of 19.3.4.

questions.question: Why must the test tasks be ones that 'the creators of the system could not have anticipated'?
questions.answer: If creators can anticipate the tasks, they can build knowledge of them into the system through data, architecture or rules. That adds task-relevant information that isn't counted, raising skill without raising generalization power, which is a form of cheating.
questions.explanation: The book says this condition is needed 'to avoid cheating.'

questions.question: Agent A solves 50 of 100 novel tasks after seeing 20 examples per task family; agent B solves 50 after seeing 2,000. Under the efficiency-ratio view, which is more intelligent, and by roughly what factor?
questions.answer: Agent A, by roughly 100 times (same operating area, 1/100 of the information).
questions.explanation: The ratio is novel situations handled per unit of information. Equal numerators and a 100x smaller denominator give a 100x larger ratio. This illustrates the book's verbal definition; the book gives no numeric formula.

questions.question: Why does the goal 'create a model that solves task X' lead to a model that does X, period?
questions.answer: Because of the shortcut rule: optimizing for skill on X will take every shortcut toward X, including adding data and task-specific knowledge, without producing generalization beyond X.
questions.explanation: The page links this goal explicitly to the shortcut rule of p.602.

questions.question: What does the green dashed vertical line in Figure 19.8 represent?
options: A fixed amount of priors + experience
The point where a system starts to overfit
questions.answer: A fixed amount of priors + experience
questions.explanation: It's labeled 'Fixed priors + experience.' The figure doesn't mark a maximum skill, overfitting, or human level.

questions.question: Can you explain, using Figure 19.8, why a large benchmark gain from training on more data doesn't necessarily mean a system became more intelligent?
questions.answer: Open-ended; a good answer says that more data moves the system right along its own curve rather than onto a higher curve.
questions.explanation: This is the key reading of the figure.
